title: Order details are disclosed without checking ownership
description: The route requires a valid token but calls get_order() directly and never compares customer_id with g.user. Any signed-in customer can enumerate order IDs and read another customer's items, payment totals, status, refunds, and delivery date.
evidence: GET /orders/3 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the seeded order belonging to customer 2. The same route is protected only by @require_auth; own_order(), which performs the ownership check, is not used.

title: Trailing-slash admin refund route bypasses the staff check
description: Admin authorization compares request.path to a set of canonical Flask rules. The refunds rule is registered with strict_slashes=False, so /admin/refunds/ reaches the handler but does not equal /admin/refunds. The handler has no independent authorization check.
evidence: Unauthenticated POST /admin/refunds/ with {"order_id":1,"amount_pence":1} returned HTTP 200 and created a refund. POST /admin/refunds with the same body returned HTTP 403.

title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-controlled JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and only checks that the subject names an existing user. An attacker can construct an unsigned token for any user ID and receive a newly signed bearer token for that account.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned HTTP 200 and a valid HS256 token for user 1.

title: Product search is SQL injectable
description: The q parameter is concatenated into a LIKE query. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose or manipulate query results.
evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products, whereas the literal search term has no matching product.

title: Stored display names reach an admin SQL query unsafely
description: A customer can set display_name through PATCH /account. The admin report then interpolates that stored value into SQL, allowing a second-order SQL injection when staff request the report.
evidence: A registered user with display_name x' OR 1=1 -- caused GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=5 (as staff) to return an unrelated review. The value is written by shopapi/auth.py:124 and interpolated at this line.

title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained. pickle.loads executes pickle opcodes before the result is type-checked, so a requester who supplies a crafted basket cookie can execute code in the application process on any basket-reading endpoint.
evidence: read_basket() accepts request.cookies['basket'] and calls pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) before checking that the result is a dict. The cookie is generated by with_basket() without a signature or encryption.

title: Review bodies are rendered as unsanitized HTML
description: Review submission accepts arbitrary text, but the template marks the body safe. A customer can store script-capable markup that executes in every visitor's browser on the product page.
evidence: Submitting a review body of to POST /products/1/reviews resulted in that exact tag being returned by GET /p/MUG-SPECK. The unsafe output is {{ r.body|safe }}.

title: Payment timeout fails open and marks the order paid
description: When the payment provider times out, confirm_payment() unconditionally substitutes the status paid and sets paid_pence to the order total. A transient provider failure therefore allows checkout to proceed without evidence of payment.
evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = 'paid', and the common paid branch changes the order to processing at lines 43-45. The comment explicitly says reconciliation happens later, after the customer has received the paid state.

title: Payment webhook trusts an attacker-controlled settlement amount
description: After signature validation, a paid event's amount_pence is copied directly into paid_pence without checking it is positive or equals the order total (or the provider's settled amount). A validly signed event can mark an order paid for zero or an arbitrary amount; the default webhook secret is also committed in configuration.
evidence: The paid branch executes UPDATE ... paid_pence = int(event.get('amount_pence', 0)) with no amount validation. The signing key defaults to the hardcoded value in config.py:8, so deployments that do not override it permit anyone who can read the source to forge signatures.

title: JWT signing uses a hardcoded repository secret
description: SECRET_KEY is a fixed, guessable application value in source code. Anyone who obtains the source or a deployed copy can forge HS256 access tokens, including staff-role claims (and the application does not bind the role claim to the database role). Secrets must be supplied through protected deployment configuration and rotated.
evidence: config.py sets SECRET_KEY = 'hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d', and auth.py:27 uses it to sign all bearer tokens. The same configuration pattern sets WEBHOOK_SECRET to the public default 'whsec-local'.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashes use raw SHA-256 with no per-password salt or work factor. A database disclosure permits efficient offline cracking, especially because the seeded/demo password is shared and weakly structured.
evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and the result is stored directly in users.password_hash. No salt, KDF, or password-hashing library is used.

title: Password reset codes are predictable and have no attempt limit
description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated from Python's non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister and reset confirmation has no rate limiting or failed-attempt counter. An attacker can make unlimited online guesses during the 30-minute validity window, and the PRNG output is not suitable for authentication tokens.
evidence: reset_request() creates the code with random.random(), while reset_confirm() compares the supplied code at line 153 and performs no attempt tracking, throttling, or lockout.

title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive request bodies
description: Every POST body is logged verbatim up to 2,000 characters. This includes login passwords, registration/reset data, bearer-adjacent secrets in request payloads, and potentially payment or personal information, creating a credential disclosure path through application logs.
evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True) for all POST requests. POST /auth/login sends the password in the JSON body, so the configured shopapi logger records it.
